# Session 6: Evaluation Metrics

## 📋 Agenda

Yesterday's question was *"do two people agree?"* Today's is **"is the model any good?"** — same tools, one column swapped.

- **Pass 1 — you build the metrics.** TP/FP/FN/TN → confusion matrix → precision, recall, F1 → Cohen's κ. No libraries.
- **Pass 2 — scikit-learn does it at scale**, on all six CEFR levels at once.
- **作戦会議** — turn today's mechanics onto your own project track.

::: {.callout-note}
**The code is on these slides.** You type it in Colab as we go — one small piece at a time, running each piece before the next. Lost? Copy the slide and rejoin.
:::

## 🎯 Learning Objectives {.smaller}

By the end of this session, you will be able to:

- Decide, for a single item, which of **TP · FP · FN · TN** it lands in — and write that as an `if`/`elif`.
- **Loop** over a labelled set, **store** one verdict per item, and **tally** the four counts.
- Build a **confusion matrix** from those counts, and read it.
- Compute **precision, recall, F1** and **Cohen's κ** *from scratch*, and say what each one answers.
- Reproduce all of it with **scikit-learn** — `classification_report`, `confusion_matrix`, `cohen_kappa_score` — on a real 6-class task.
- Interpret the numbers critically: what a high or low score does and **doesn't** tell you.

# How today works — two passes

We use the **CEFR-SP** set from S5: 72 sentences, 12 per level, and a model's frozen predictions for each.

|  | **Pass 1 — you build it** | **Pass 2 — scikit-learn** |
|--|--|--|
| **Question** | "Is this sentence **advanced**?" (yes/no) | "Which level — A1…C2?" |
| **Cells to track** | **4** | **36** |
| **Tools** | `for`, `if`, dictionaries | `classification_report`, `confusion_matrix`, `cohen_kappa_score` |

## Why binary first
Four cells you can count on your fingers. Everything you build in pass 1 is **exactly** what scikit-learn does in pass 2 — six times over, once per level.
:::

## Today runs on *frozen* predictions {.smaller}

No API key, no live model. The model was run **once**, offline, and its answers committed to a file.

- On Day 1 you saw the model's answers **change from run to run**.
- When you're learning to *measure* quality, that wobble is noise fighting the lesson.
- So today **everyone's precision, recall, F1 and κ come out identical**. If your number differs from the slide, you have a bug — not a different model.

# Pass 1 · Step 1 — collapse to one yes/no question

## Six levels → one question {.smaller}

CEFR has six levels. For pass 1 we ask **one** thing:

> **Is this sentence *advanced* — C1 or C2?**

- `"yes"` = C1 or C2 → this is our **positive class**
- `"no"`  = A1, A2, B1, B2

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
**Choosing the positive class is a decision, not a technicality.** "Precision" and "recall" are always *about the positive class*. Change what counts as positive and every number changes. In your project, say out loud which class is positive before you report a score.
:::

# Pass 1 · Step 2 — ask one item

## Open Colab and look at one item {.smaller}

The 12 rows are already in the notebook, as a list of dictionaries — the same `{id, text, …}` shape you have used since Day 1, with two extra keys:

```python
item = items[0]                     # the first of the 12 rows
print(item["gold"], item["pred"])   # its gold answer, then the model's
```

. . .

```
no no
```

Row 17: the gold says not advanced, and the model agrees. **One item, two labels** — that is all a metric ever looks at.

## Ask it the first question {.smaller}

Is this item a **true positive**? That means *both* labels are `"yes"`:

```python
# `and` means BOTH sides have to be true:
if item["gold"] == "yes" and item["pred"] == "yes":
    print("TP")     # only runs when both are "yes"
```

. . .

```

```

**Nothing printed.** Not a bug — the honest answer. Row 17 is not a TP, and one `if` can only ever answer *one* of the four questions.

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
An `if` with no `else` is silent when the condition is false. To classify **every** item we need all four questions, and exactly one of them must fire.
:::

# Pass 1 · Step 3 — the four branches

## The 2×2 table, written as `if`/`elif` {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="42%"}
|            | pred **yes** | pred **no** |
|------------|:------------:|:-----------:|
| gold **yes** | **TP** | **FN** |
| gold **no**  | **FP** | **TN** |

Four cells. Four branches. **Same order.**
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
```python
# checked top to bottom; the FIRST match wins, so exactly one branch runs:
if item["gold"] == "yes" and item["pred"] == "yes":
    print("TP")      # advanced, and the model agreed
elif item["gold"] == "no" and item["pred"] == "yes":
    print("FP")      # a false alarm
elif item["gold"] == "yes" and item["pred"] == "no":
    print("FN")      # a real one, missed
else:
    print("TN")      # not advanced, left alone
```
:::

::::

. . .

`elif` = *"only if none of the above matched."* The branches are checked top to bottom and **exactly one** runs — so every item lands in exactly one cell. The final `else` needs no condition: if it isn't TP, FP or FN, it can only be TN.

Change which item you look at and re-run:

```python

print(item["gold"], item["pred"])
```

```

```

. . .

The gold says not advanced; the model said advanced. Branch 1 fails, branch 2 matches:


# Pass 1 · Step 4 — make it a function

## Twelve items, one rule {.smaller}

You are about to ask that same question of all 12 rows. Copying the ladder twelve times would be absurd — so **name it once**:

```python
def outcome(gold_label, pred_label):
    """Which of the four cells does this one item land in?"""
    if gold_label == "yes" and pred_label == "yes":
        return "TP"      # `return` hands the answer back, instead of printing it
    elif gold_label == "no" and pred_label == "yes":
        return "FP"
    elif gold_label == "yes" and pred_label == "no":
        return "FN"
    else:
        return "TN"
```

. . .

Two changes from step 3, and only two: it is **wrapped in `def`**, and every `print` became a **`return`**.

## `print` shows you · `return` hands it back {.smaller}

```python
print(outcome("yes", "no"))     # gold said advanced, model said no → a miss
```

. . .

```
FN
```

. . .

- **`print`** puts a value on the screen and then it is *gone*.
- **`return`** hands the value back to whoever called the function, so you can **keep it, store it, count it**. That is exactly what step 5 needs.

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
**Test it by hand before you trust it.** `outcome("yes", "no")` — gold says advanced, model said no → a **miss** → `FN` ✓. Try all four combinations against the table. A function you have not checked is a guess.
:::

# Pass 1 · Step 5 — loop, and store every decision

## One verdict per sentence {.smaller}

Now run that function over all 12 rows and **keep** the answers — the same "build a list in a loop" pattern you wrote on Day 1:

```python
decisions = []                     # start empty; the loop fills it
for item in items:                 # one pass per row of the table
    decisions.append(outcome(item["gold"], item["pred"]))   # add its verdict

print(decisions)                   # 12 verdicts, in the table's order
```

. . .

```
['TN', 'TP', 'TN', 'TN', 'TP', 'FN', 'TN', 'FN', 'TN', 'TN', 'TP', 'FP']
```

. . .

Twelve items in, twelve verdicts out — **in the same order as the table**. Position 6 is `'FN'`: that's row 22, the racing-bicycle sentence the model missed.

## Why store them, rather than just count? {.smaller}

We could have counted as we went. We keep the list because **the list is the evidence**.

- A metric is a *summary*. `decisions` is the thing being summarised — you can always go back to it.
- Every `'FN'` and `'FP'` in that list points at a **specific sentence** you can read and argue about.
- That is **error analysis**, and it is where the real research questions live: *is this the model's fault, or my scheme's?*

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
Later today `show_errors()` does exactly this for you on the 6-class task — it filters the items whose verdict was wrong and prints them. You have just built its engine.
:::

# Pass 1 · Step 6 — tally the verdicts

## Count the four outcomes {.smaller}

This is Day 1's `count_labels` exercise, run on a new list:

```python
tally = {}                         # a dict: verdict -> how many times
for d in decisions:                # d is "TP", "FP", "FN" or "TN"
    tally[d] = tally.get(d, 0) + 1   # count so far (0 if new), plus one

print(tally)
```

. . .

```
{'TN': 6, 'TP': 3, 'FN': 2, 'FP': 1}
```

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
`tally.get(d, 0)` means *"how many so far — and if you've never seen this one, start from 0."* Without the `.get`, the very first `'TN'` would crash, because `tally["TN"]` does not exist yet.
:::

. . .

**Compare to the numbers you counted by hand in step 1: TP = 3, FP = 1, FN = 2, TN = 6.** They match. Your code and your eyes agree.

# Pass 1 · Step 7 — the confusion matrix

## The tally, arranged {.smaller}

A confusion matrix is **not a new calculation**. It is those same four numbers, put in a square so you can *see* them:

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
```python
show_2x2(tally)
```

```
          pred yes  pred no
gold yes         3        2
gold no          1        6
```
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
- The **diagonal** (3 and 6) is everything the model got right — 9 of 12.
- The **off-diagonal** (2 and 1) is everything it got wrong, **split by direction**.
- Two errors are *misses*; one is a *false alarm*. A single accuracy figure would hide that difference completely.
:::

::::

. . .

**Look at the matrix before you compute anything.** The shape of the errors is the finding; the metrics just put a number on it.

## Row totals, column totals {.smaller}

The margins matter — you need them for κ in step 9:

|              | pred **yes** | pred **no** | **total** |
|--------------|:------------:|:-----------:|:---------:|
| gold **yes** | 3 | 2 | **5** ← the gold set has 5 advanced sentences |
| gold **no**  | 1 | 6 | **7** |
| **total**    | **4** | **8** | **12** |

. . .

- **Rows** = what the gold says. **Columns** = what the model says.
- Gold called 5 sentences advanced; the model called only **4**. It is slightly **stingy** with the positive label.
- Watch that habit — in pass 2 it becomes the most visible thing about this model.

# Pass 1 · Step 8 — precision, recall, F1

## Precision — of what it flagged, how much was right? {.smaller}

**Numbers first**, so you can check it on paper:

```python
print(3 / (3 + 1))            # TP / (TP + FP)
```

```
0.75
```

. . .

**Same thing, read off the tally** — so it survives a change of data:

```python
print(tally["TP"] / (tally["TP"] + tally["FP"]))    # the same, from the tally
```

```
0.75
```

. . .

Of the 4 sentences the model *called* advanced, 3 really were. **Precision = 0.75.**

## Precision — now as a function {.smaller}

```python
def precision(tally):
    """Of everything CALLED advanced, how much really was?  TP / (TP + FP)"""
    tp = tally.get("TP", 0)      # .get(..., 0) so a missing count reads as 0
    fp = tally.get("FP", 0)
    if tp + fp == 0:             # the model never said "yes" at all
        return 0.0               # no credit earned — and no division by zero
    return tp / (tp + fp)        # everything it got right, over everything it claimed

print(round(precision(tally), 3))   # round to 3 decimal places
```

. . .

```
0.75
```

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
## Always guard the denominator
If a model never predicts the positive class, `TP + FP` is **0** and Python raises `ZeroDivisionError`. Returning `0.0` says *"it earned no credit"* — which is the honest reading. Every metric you write today gets this guard.
:::

## Recall — your turn {.smaller}

Recall asks the **other** question: *of everything that truly was advanced, how much did we catch?*

$$R = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$$

```python
def recall(tally):
    """Of everything that TRULY was advanced, how much did we find?"""
    tp = tally.get("TP", 0)
    fn = tally.get("FN", 0)       # ← the only real change
    if tp + fn == 0:              # nothing was truly advanced — nothing to find
        return 0.0
    return tp / (tp + fn)         # what it found, over everything there was to find

print(round(recall(tally), 3))
```

. . .

```
0.6
```

Three of the five genuinely advanced sentences were found. **Recall = 0.60.**

## F1 — one number, no hiding {.smaller}

Precision and recall pull against each other: flag everything and recall hits 1.0 while precision collapses. **F1** is the harmonic mean, so a high score cannot cover for a low one:

$$F_1 = 2 \cdot \frac{P \cdot R}{P + R}$$

```python
def f1(tally):
    """Harmonic mean of precision and recall."""
    p = precision(tally)         # reuse the function you just wrote
    r = recall(tally)            # ...and the other one
    if p + r == 0:               # both zero — nothing to average
        return 0.0
    return 2 * p * r / (p + r)   # harmonic mean: a low score drags it down

print(round(precision(tally), 3), round(recall(tally), 3), round(f1(tally), 3))
```

. . .

```
0.75 0.6 0.667
```

## What 0.75 vs. 0.60 actually says {.smaller}

The gap between precision and recall **is a description of the model's personality**:

- **Precision 0.75 > Recall 0.60** → the model is **conservative** about calling something advanced. When it commits, it is usually right; but it lets real C1s slip past as B2.
- The two it missed (rows 22, 24) were both **C1 → B2** — near misses, not wild errors.

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
## Which error can you live with?
That is a **research design** question, not a statistics one.

- Screening texts for a C1 reading list? A **miss** (FN) is expensive — favour recall.
- Making a claim in a paper about which sentences are advanced? A **false alarm** (FP) is expensive — favour precision.

Say which one your project cares about *before* you report a score.
:::

# Pass 1 · Step 9 — Cohen's κ

## Why accuracy isn't enough {.smaller}

Start with the easy number — **observed agreement**, the diagonal over the total:

```python
n = tally["TP"] + tally["FP"] + tally["FN"] + tally["TN"]   # all 12 items
p_o = (tally["TP"] + tally["TN"]) / n   # the diagonal (both agreed), over the total
print(round(p_o, 3))
```

. . .

```
0.75
```

. . .

Gold and model agree on 9 of 12 items. Sounds decent — but **so would a lazy model that answered "no" to everything**: it would score 7/12 without knowing anything at all. Raw agreement flatters whoever plays the odds.

## Agreement you'd get by luck {.smaller}

$p_e$ = the agreement two raters would hit **by chance**, given how often each one uses each label. Multiply their rates, label by label — the row and column totals from step 7:

```python
# each line: how often GOLD says it × how often the MODEL says it = agreement by luck
p_yes = ((tally["TP"] + tally["FN"]) / n) * ((tally["TP"] + tally["FP"]) / n)
p_no  = ((tally["FP"] + tally["TN"]) / n) * ((tally["FN"] + tally["TN"]) / n)
p_e   = p_yes + p_no          # luck on "yes" plus luck on "no"
print(round(p_yes, 3), round(p_no, 3), round(p_e, 3))
```

. . .

```
0.139 0.389 0.528
```

. . .

- `p_yes`: gold says yes **5/12** × model says yes **4/12** = 0.139
- `p_no`: gold says no **7/12** × model says no **8/12** = 0.389
- **More than half** the agreement we observed (0.75) was available for free.

## κ — the honest number {.smaller}

$$\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}$$

*How much of the agreement that luck couldn't explain did they actually achieve?*

```python
# what they beat luck by (p_o - p_e), over how much was left to beat (1 - p_e):
print(round((p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e), 3))
```

. . .

```
0.471
```

. . .

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
| Cohen's κ | Landis & Koch | McHugh |
|:---------:|:--------------|:-------|
| 0.21–0.40 | Fair | Minimal |
| **0.41–0.60** | **Moderate** | **Weak** |
| 0.61–0.80 | Substantial | Moderate |
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**75% agreement → κ = 0.47.**

The same gap S4 showed you (80% → κ ≈ 0.52), now computed by your own code.
:::

::::

## Wrap it up — and notice what you've built {.smaller}

```python
def kappa(tally):
    """Agreement corrected for chance: (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e)."""
    n = tally["TP"] + tally["FP"] + tally["FN"] + tally["TN"]   # every item
    p_o = (tally["TP"] + tally["TN"]) / n     # agreement we actually observed
    p_yes = ((tally["TP"] + tally["FN"]) / n) * ((tally["TP"] + tally["FP"]) / n)
    p_no = ((tally["FP"] + tally["TN"]) / n) * ((tally["FN"] + tally["TN"]) / n)
    p_e = p_yes + p_no                        # agreement luck alone would give
    if 1 - p_e == 0:                          # luck already explains everything
        return 0.0
    return (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e)            # how much of the rest they achieved
```

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## This is yesterday's function
Nothing in `kappa()` knows whether column two came from **your partner** or **a model**. That is why S5's agreement number and today's evaluation number are the same statistic: **κ measures two label columns, whoever produced them.**
:::

# Pass 2 · The real task, with scikit-learn

## Six levels, thirty-six cells {.smaller}

Drop the yes/no simplification. The actual task is: **A1 · A2 · B1 · B2 · C1 · C2**.

- **4 cells → 36.** Counting by hand stops being reasonable.
- Precision and recall are always *about one positive class* — so with six classes you get **six** precisions, **six** recalls, **six** F1s.
- The trick is small: to score `C1`, treat **`C1` as "yes" and all five others as "no"** — pass 1, run six times. That is called **one-vs-rest**, and it is all `classification_report` does.

. . .

```python
# ordered=True: the six levels sit on a scale, so also report weighted κ
evaluate(gold, predictions, ordered=True)
```

`ordered=True` says these labels sit on a **scale** — which changes which κ you should read. Hold that thought.

## Read the report {.smaller}

```
              precision    recall  f1-score   support

          A1       0.75      0.25      0.38        12
          A2       0.35      0.58      0.44        12
          B1       0.36      0.33      0.35        12
          B2       0.37      0.58      0.45        12
          C1       0.35      0.50      0.41        12
          C2       1.00      0.08      0.15        12

    accuracy                           0.39        72
   macro avg       0.53      0.39      0.36        72
```

. . .

- Every **row** is one pass-1 run: for `C1`, TP/FP/FN/TN with C1 as the positive class.
- **`support`** = how many gold items that class has — 12 each, by design.
- **`macro avg`** = the plain average of the six F1s. Every class counts equally, **however rare it is** — which is why it is the honest headline for an imbalanced set.

## Brace yourself: accuracy is 39% {.smaller}

Before concluding the model is useless — **look at *how* it is wrong.**

. . .

- **97% of its answers are within one level** of the gold label.
- Only two sentences in the whole set miss by two. **Nothing misses by more.**
- A model that had no idea would scatter A1s against C2s. This one does not.

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
**"Right idea, imprecise thresholds"** is a completely different failure from **"doesn't understand the task"** — and no single accuracy number can tell them apart. That is what the confusion matrix is for.
:::

## The confusion matrix — read *down the columns* {.smaller}

|  | pred A1 | pred A2 | pred B1 | pred B2 | pred C1 | pred C2 |
|--|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| **gold A1** | **3** | 9 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **gold A2** | 1 | **7** | 4 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **gold B1** | 0 | 4 | **4** | 4 | 0 | 0 |
| **gold B2** | 0 | 0 | 3 | **7** | 2 | 0 |
| **gold C1** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 6 | **6** | 0 |
| **gold C2** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 9 | **1** |
| **column total** | **4** | **20** | **11** | **19** | **17** | **1** |

. . .

Rows are gold, so *rows* tell you what happened to each true level. But read **down the columns** — how often the model *says* each level. The gold set is **balanced, 12 per level**, so an unbiased rater would use each label about 12 times.

## Central-tendency bias {.smaller}

The model said **A2 twenty times** and **A1 four times**. It said **C2 exactly once** — in 72 chances.

. . .

- Everything is squeezed toward the **middle** of the scale; the extremes are avoided.
- Why would a rater — human or machine — under pressure to judge something as fuzzy as "difficulty" **drift to the middle and refuse to commit to the ends**?
- This is your pass-1 finding again: with "advanced" as positive, precision 0.89 but recall 0.67. **It under-uses the top of the scale.**

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
You will meet this tendency in **your own annotation** — and in your teammates'. It is one of the first things to check in a scheme that isn't reaching acceptable κ.
:::

## Two κ values, same data {.smaller}

`evaluate(..., ordered=True)` printed both, right under the report:

```
Cohen's kappa            0.267
Cohen's kappa (weighted) 0.849   <- labels are ordered
```

. . .

**Plain κ = 0.27** ("fair" / "minimal") — because plain κ treats **A1 → A2 as exactly as wrong as A1 → C2**.

**Quadratic-weighted κ = 0.85** — because CEFR levels are **ordinal**, and a near miss *should* hurt less:

$$w_{ij} = \frac{(i-j)^2}{(N-1)^2}$$

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
## Report the one that matches your labels
Same predictions, 0.27 or 0.85 depending on a single argument. **Ordered labels → weighted κ. Unordered categories → plain κ.** State which you used and why; a κ without that sentence is unreadable. *(Arase et al. reported weighted κ = .628 on this task.)*
:::

## Error analysis — the model's fault, or the scheme's? {.smaller}

```python
errors = show_errors(gold, predictions)   # a table of every item it got wrong
errors.head(15)     # ...or errors[errors["gold"] == "C2"] to see the hard end
```

44 misses — too many to read one by one, and you don't need to. **Skim a dozen**, then look hard at the rows where gold is **C2** or **A1**: the ends of the scale are where the arguments are.

. . .

For each miss you read, ask:

1. Is the **gold** defensible here, or is this genuinely borderline?
2. Would **you and your partner** have agreed on this sentence?
3. Would a **better-written scheme** have prevented this error?

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
Remember rows 19, 23 and 25 — the three obituary sentences. In pass 1's yes/no world the model got all three *right*. In six classes it called every one of them A2 instead of A1. **The question you ask determines the error you can see.**
:::

# 作戦会議 — Day-2 strategy huddle

## Turn today onto your own track {.smaller}

Everything this week has run on CEFR-SP. Your project doesn't. Spend the next **~12 minutes** with your team adding three things to your **作戦シート**:

1. **A draft annotation scheme** — your label set, plus **one line of guideline per label**. (Steps ①②.)
2. **Your gold source** — the provided pool, or one you build yourselves? Who annotates, and how many items? (Step ③.)
3. **The agreement you'd accept** — a κ number, decided **now**, before you see any results. And: **which class is positive**, and whether your labels are **ordered** (→ weighted κ) or not.

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
Point 3 is the one teams skip and regret. A threshold chosen *after* seeing the number is not a threshold — it's a rationalisation.
:::
